title: Privilege Escalation via Missing Access Control

steps.description: Attacker analyzes the contract's ABI and bytecode, discovering that emergencyWithdraw() is an external function without the onlyOwner modifier. While setFeeRecipient() and setWithdrawalLimit() are properly protected, this critical function was accidentally left open — a common copy-paste error during development.

Attacker calls the unprotected emergencyWithdraw function, passing WETH as the token and the entire contract balance as the amount. Since there is no access control check, the transaction succeeds and transfers all 5,000 ETH to the attacker's address.

state_changes.withdrawal_limit_bypass: ⚠️ 100 ETH/day limit irrelevant — emergencyWithdraw has none

steps.description: The legitimate owner detects the unauthorized withdrawal through monitoring alerts, but the funds are already gone. Even if the contract has a pause mechanism, it cannot recover the stolen funds. The owner can only prevent further damage to any remaining tokens.

state_changes.remaining_tokens: ✓ Any non-WETH tokens are safe (if pause works)

steps.description: Attacker launders the $10M through DEX swaps, cross-chain bridges, and mixing services. The root cause — a missing onlyOwner modifier on a single function — resulted in total loss of funds. This class of vulnerability is preventable with automated access control audits and comprehensive test coverage.

state_changes.lesson: Every privileged function must have explicit access control
